A.claim: A signed-in non-admin could view or change benefit start dates through GET and POST /benefits if the admin middleware were missing; an earlier change wired it on both routes, and non-admin and anonymous requests are redirected to /login while the admin still gets the page.
When a signed-in non-admin requests an admin-only route, the admin middleware answers with a redirect to /login rather than an HTTP 403 status.

Any signed-in user can read another user's first and last name and stock, fund and bond allocation percentages by requesting GET /allocations/:userId with that user's id, because the handler takes the id from the URL parameter instead of the session and the route only checks that the caller is signed in; ids are sequential integers, so every user can be listed.

A signed-in user can read other users' allocations through the threshold query parameter of the allocations page, because the allocations data-access code inserts threshold into a MongoDB $where expression that a crafted value can make true for every record, and reading the user id from the session does not stop this.

Every signed-in user can read all memos on /memos, including those posted by other users; memo records hold only the text and a timestamp with no owner, so the page is a shared board and holds no per-user data.

An anonymous caller could sign in as another user by sending a MongoDB operator object as userName in a JSON login body; the operator does select a user record, but the submitted password is then compared with strict equality, so the login fails.

A signed-in non-admin could get past the admin check on /benefits by changing the path case, adding a trailing slash or query string, using HEAD, or posting a JSON body; every variant that matches the route runs the admin middleware and is redirected to /login, the other variants return 404, and the benefits data-access code is used only by the benefits route.

The login handler keeps the session id issued before login instead of issuing a new one (signup does issue a new one), so a session id obtained before sign-in stays valid afterwards; whether an attacker can plant such an id in a victim's browser is not settled.
The login handler returns different error messages for an unknown username and for a wrong password.
The session cookie is configured without a maxAge, so sessions do not expire.

The profile and contributions handlers, for both reading and updating, take the user id from the session and the data-access code filters on it, so a signed-in user cannot read or change another user's profile or contributions through them.
The root route has no middleware but its handler checks the session itself and sends anonymous callers away, and both / and /dashboard use only the user id stored in the session.
A new user could make themselves admin at signup if the user record accepted arbitrary request fields; signup builds the record from explicit fields and never sets isAdmin.

Anonymous callers could reach the pages meant for signed-in users (dashboard, profile, contributions, allocations, memos, learn, research) if the login middleware were missing; each of those routes is wired with it, it checks that a user id is present in the session, and anonymous requests are redirected to /login.
The tutorial pages are reachable without signing in, and they and the error page render no user data.
A signed-in user could make themselves admin through the profile update if it wrote arbitrary request fields; the update builds its $set from a fixed list of fields.
The admin middleware reads the admin flag from the database on every request and denies access when the lookup fails or finds no user.
The app is served over plain HTTP and the session cookie is HttpOnly but not marked Secure, so an attacker on the network path can read the session cookie.
User passwords are stored and compared in plaintext.
Any signed-in user can run code in the server process through the contributions form, because the handler passes form field values to eval.
The research route sends an outbound request to a URL built from query-string parameters, so a caller can choose where the server sends requests.
The /learn route redirects to whatever URL is given in the url query parameter.
The profile handler uses a regular expression that can backtrack excessively on crafted input.
The login handler writes the submitted username to the log without escaping it.

No cross-site request forgery protection runs before the routes because the csurf middleware is commented out, so a page an admin visits could submit POST /benefits with the admin's session and change benefit dates for someone who cannot pass the admin check.
Template autoescaping is turned off in the view engine setup.

B.claim: A signed-in non-admin could view or change other users' benefit start dates through GET and POST /benefits if the admin middleware were missing; an earlier change wired it on both routes, non-admin GET and POST requests (form-encoded or JSON) are redirected to /login and leave the target user's date unchanged, and the admin still reaches the page.
When a signed-in non-admin requests an admin-only route, the admin middleware answers with a redirect to /login rather than an HTTP 403 status.

Any signed-in user, including a freshly self-registered account, can read another user's first and last name and stock, fund and bond allocation percentages by requesting GET /allocations/:userId with that user's id, because the handler takes the id from the URL instead of the session and the route only checks that the caller is signed in; ids are sequential and anyone can sign up, so every user's allocation can be listed.

Every signed-in user can read and post to the memo board on /memos; memos are stored with only text and a timestamp and no author or recipient, and no route edits or deletes a memo, so no user's own data is reachable there.

A signed-in user could grant themselves admin through the profile update if it wrote arbitrary request fields; the update sets only seven named fields, and a JSON profile update carrying isAdmin, _id and userId changed no admin flag.
A new user could grant themselves admin at signup if the user record accepted arbitrary request fields; signup builds the record from named fields only.

A signed-in non-admin could get past the admin check on /benefits through path case, a trailing slash, a query string, HEAD, or a JSON POST body; Express matches these to the same route and middleware, there is no method-override middleware, and every variant is redirected to /login with the target user's date unchanged.
The admin middleware does not handle the error from its user lookup, but on error the user is empty, so the admin test is false and the request is redirected instead of passed through.
The profile and contributions handlers take the user id from the session and the data-access code filters on it, so a signed-in user cannot reach another user's profile or contributions through them.

A signed-in user can read every user's allocations from their own allocations page through the threshold query parameter, because the allocations data-access code splices threshold into a MongoDB $where string, and reading the user id from the session does not stop this.

The browser test that guards the admin check on /benefits only tries a non-admin GET, so removing the admin middleware from the POST /benefits route would let non-admins change other users' benefit dates again without that test failing.
The same /benefits guard test never checks that the non-admin sign-in succeeded, and a failed sign-in also ends on /login, so the test can pass without exercising the admin check.
The root route has no middleware but its handler checks the session itself, and /dashboard renders only the record of the user in the session.

Anonymous callers could reach /dashboard, /profile, /contributions, /allocations, /memos, /learn and /research if the login middleware were missing; each is wired with it, and it checks that a user id is present in the session.
The tutorial pages are public static pages reachable without signing in and show no user data.
Static files under app/assets are served to anyone without login, and none of them shadows a route that requires login or admin rights.
The session secret under config/ was not assessed; express-session keeps session data on the server and signs only the session id.

The existing end-to-end allocation tests sign in as user1 and visit /allocations/1, the admin's page, so the test suite treats reading another user's allocations as normal and would either break under a fix that rejects foreign ids or keep passing without testing the user's own page.
Any signed-in user can run code on the server through the contributions form, because the handler passes req.body.preTax, afterTax and roth to eval.
The research route calls needle.get on a URL taken from the query string, so a caller can make the server request addresses of its choosing.
The /learn route redirects to a URL taken from the request without checking it.
The login lookup takes userName from a request body that may be JSON, so an operator object could select a user record, but the password is compared with strict equality, which limits the effect.
The login handler does not regenerate the session after a successful login.

Cross-site request forgery protection is commented out, so a page on another site can make an admin's browser send POST /benefits and change benefit dates through the admin's session without failing the admin check.
The session cookie security flags are commented out in the server setup.
Autoescaping in the swig template engine is disabled.
A memo can carry script that is stored and later runs in the browser of every user who views the memos page, including the admin.
User passwords are stored in plaintext.
The profile update stores social security numbers in plaintext.
The profile handler uses a regular expression that can backtrack excessively on crafted input.
The login handler returns different errors for an unknown username and for a wrong password, which reveals which usernames exist.
The allocations data-access code invokes its callback a second time.
